claim: Yellow Fever is estimated to cause 78,000 deaths a year in Africa alone.
source: Yellow Fever (YF) is an arbovirus endemic in tropical regions of South America and Africa and it is estimated to cause 78,000 deaths a year in Africa alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Garske et al., 2014 as indicated in the introduction section.

claim: In the least severe climate change scenario (RCP 2.6), there is a 93.0% [95%CI(92.7, 93.2%)] chance that annual deaths will increase in 2050.
source: In the least severe scenario, we find a 93.0%[95%CI(92.7, 93.2%)] chance that annual deaths will increase in 2050.
evidence: This claim is supported by the model projections and statistical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Yellow Fever is responsible for approximately 78,000 deaths per year, although under reporting is high.
source: It is responsible for approximately 78,000 deaths per year, although under reporting is high and since YF has a non-specific symptom set, misdiagnosis is an issue (Garske et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Garske et al., 2014.

claim: Yellow Fever has three transmission 'cycles' in Africa: urban, zoonotic and intermediate.
source: YF has three transmission 'cycles' in Africa: urban, zoonotic and intermediate.
evidence: This is established knowledge about YF transmission patterns.

claim: The urban cycle of Yellow Fever is mediated by Aedes Aegypti mosquitoes.
source: The urban cycle, mediated by Aedes Aegypti mosquitoes, is responsible for explosive outbreaks such as the one seen in Angola in 2016 (Ingelbeen et al., 2018; Wilder-Smith and Monath, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ingelbeen et al., 2018 and Wilder-Smith and Monath, 2017.

claim: The majority of YF infections are thought to occur as a result of zoonotic spillover from the sylvatic reservoir in non-human primates.
source: While the urban cycle can rapidly amplify transmission, the majority of YF infections are thought to occur as a result of zoonotic spillover from the sylvatic reservoir in non-human primates (NHP).
evidence: This is established knowledge about YF transmission dynamics.

claim: The zoonotic cycle of Yellow Fever is mediated by a variety of mosquito vectors including Aedes africanus.
source: This zoonotic cycle is mediated by a variety of mosquito vectors including Aedes africanus and, as the NHP hosts are mostly unaffected by the infection in Africa, the force of infection due to spillover is fairly constant, although land use change has been shown to affect this (Monath and Vasconcelos, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Monath and Vasconcelos, 2015.

claim: NHP hosts are mostly unaffected by Yellow Fever infection in Africa.
source: This zoonotic cycle is mediated by a variety of mosquito vectors including Aedes africanus and, as the NHP hosts are mostly unaffected by the infection in Africa, the force of infection due to spillover is fairly constant, although land use change has been shown to affect this (Monath and Vasconcelos, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Monath and Vasconcelos, 2015.

claim: Land use change has been shown to affect the force of infection due to zoonotic spillover.
source: This zoonotic cycle is mediated by a variety of mosquito vectors including Aedes africanus and, as the NHP hosts are mostly unaffected by the infection in Africa, the force of infection due to spillover is fairly constant, although land use change has been shown to affect this (Monath and Vasconcelos, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Monath and Vasconcelos, 2015.

claim: The intermediate cycle of Yellow Fever is sometimes called the savannah cycle and is mediated by mosquitoes such as Ae. luteocephalus.
source: The intermediate cycle is sometimes called the savannah cycle and is mediated by mosquitoes such as Ae. luteocephalus, who feed opportunistically on humans and NHP, although human-human transmission is limited (Barrett and Higgs, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barrett and Higgs, 2007.

claim: Global mean temperatures are likely to rise by 1.5°C, compared with pre-industrial levels, by between 2030 and 2052 if current trends continue.
source: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) states that global mean temperatures are likely to rise by 1.5°C, compared with pre-industrial levels, by between 2030 and 2052 if current trends continue (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Masson-Delmotte et al., 2018.

claim: Increases are projected not only in mean temperature but also in the extremes of temperature, extremes of precipitation and the probability of drought.
source: Increases are projected not only in mean temperature but also in the extremes of temperature, extremes of precipitation and the probability of drought (Kharin et al., 2013; Dunning et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kharin et al., 2013 and Dunning et al., 2018.

claim: Projected climate change will alter the global distribution of A. aegypti and thus, the risk of diseases it carries.
source: Focusing on the main urban vector, A. aegypti, there is strong evidence that projected climate change will alter its global distribution and thus, the risk of diseases it carries (Ryan et al., 2019; World Health Organisation, 2018; World Health Organisation, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ryan et al., 2019 and World Health Organisation, 2018.

claim: Climate change has been predicted to increase the regions at risk from dengue and Zika transmission.
source: Climate change has been predicted to increase the regions at risk from dengue and Zika transmission, although seasonal variation in temperature may mitigate the likelihood of outbreaks in areas at the edges of the endemic zone (Mordecai et al., 2017; Huber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mordecai et al., 2017 and Huber et al., 2018.

claim: Seasonal variation in temperature may mitigate the likelihood of outbreaks in areas at the edges of the endemic zone.
source: Climate change has been predicted to increase the regions at risk from dengue and Zika transmission, although seasonal variation in temperature may mitigate the likelihood of outbreaks in areas at the edges of the endemic zone (Mordecai et al., 2017; Huber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mordecai et al., 2017 and Huber et al., 2018.

claim: The model predicts a high probability of YF report in West Africa and reflects the general patterns of YF occurrence.
source: The model predicts a high probability of YF report in these areas and reflects the general patterns of YF occurrence, see Figure 1 for comparison.
evidence: This is supported by the model results and Figure 1 showing occurrence data and predictions.

claim: The model fit can be characterised by the Area Under the Curve (AUC) statistic which was 0.9004.
source: Model fit can be characterised by the Area Under the Curve (AUC) statistic (Huang and Ling, 2005), which was 0.9004, similar to the original model formulation of Garske et al., 2014.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of model fit with citation to Huang and Ling, 2005 and comparison to Garske et al., 2014.

claim: The AUC of 0.9004 is similar to the original model formulation of Garske et al., 2014.
source: Model fit can be characterised by the Area Under the Curve (AUC) statistic (Huang and Ling, 2005), which was 0.9004, similar to the original model formulation of Garske et al., 2014.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work cited as Garske et al., 2014.

claim: Nigeria and South Sudan have high temperature suitability for YF transmission.
source: This highlights the high suitability of countries such as Nigeria and South Sudan for YF transmission.
evidence: This is supported by the temperature suitability model results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Rwanda, Burundi and areas of Mali and Mauritania have low average temperature suitability for YF transmission.
source: In contrast, Rwanda, Burundi and areas of Mali and Mauritania have low average temperature suitability.
evidence: This is supported by the temperature suitability model results shown in Figure 2.

claim: In West Africa, the predicted change in force of infection is clustered around zero in the majority of scenarios, particularly for year 2050.
source: In West Africa, the predicted change is clustered around zero in the majority of scenarios; this is particularly the case for year 2050.
evidence: This is supported by the model projections shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the East and Central regions of Africa, a predicted increase in force of infection is more apparent.
source: In the East and Central regions, a predicted increase in force of infection is more apparent.
evidence: This is supported by the model projections shown in Figure 4.

claim: For RCP 2.6 Guinea Bissau, the change in force of infection in 2070 is 10.3% (95%CrI [−33.2% , 96.3%]).
source: For RCP 2.6 Guinea Bissau, the change in force of infection in 2070 is potentially broad, with a credible interval spanning zero: 10.3% (95%CrI [−33.2% , 96.3%]).
evidence: This is supported by the model projections for specific countries.

claim: In Central African Republic, there is a notable increase in force of infection by 87.1% (95%CrI [12.4% , 390.2%]) for RCP 2.6 in 2070.
source: Whereas in Central African Republic, there is a notable increase by 87.1% (95%CrI [12.4% , 390.2%]).
evidence: This is supported by the model projections for specific countries.

claim: The projections assume vaccination is static from 2019 onwards, meaning only routine vaccination continues at 2018 levels.
source: These projections assume vaccination is static from 2019 onwards that is that only routine vaccination continues at 2018 levels.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption stated in the methods.

claim: The projections assume case management is unvarying.
source: Similarly, we assume case management is unvarying.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption stated in the methods.

claim: The probability that deaths will increase is 95.5% (95% CrI [95.3%, 95.7%]) for RCP 2.6 in year 2070.
source: The probability that deaths will increase is 95.5% (95% CrI [95.3%, 95.7%]) for RCP 2.6 in year 2070, rising to 95.9% (95% CrI [95.7%, 96.1%]) for RCP 8.5 in year 2070, values for all scenarios and years are shown in appendix 1.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of model projections.

claim: The probability that deaths will increase is 95.9% (95% CrI [95.7%, 96.1%]) for RCP 8.5 in year 2070.
source: The probability that deaths will increase is 95.5% (95% CrI [95.3%, 95.7%]) for RCP 2.6 in year 2070, rising to 95.9% (95% CrI [95.7%, 96.1%]) for RCP 8.5 in year 2070, values for all scenarios and years are shown in appendix 1.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of model projections.

claim: The most severe increases in burden are seen for RCP scenario 8.5, especially in year 2070.
source: As with the force of infection projections, the most severe increases are seen for RCP scenario 8.5, especially in year 2070.
evidence: This is supported by the model projections shown in Table 1 and figures.

claim: The most marked increases in burden are found in East and central Africa.
source: As such, it appears that the most marked increases in burden are found in East and central Africa.
evidence: This is supported by the model projections shown in Figure 5 and related figures.

claim: The four countries with the least distinct change in burden are Liberia, Guinea, Sierra Leone and the Gambia, all in West Africa.
source: The four countries with the least distinct change, Liberia, Guinea, Sierra Leone and the Gambia, are all in West Africa, commonly thought to see the most intense YF transmission.
evidence: This is supported by the model projections shown in Figure 5.

claim: The force of infection is projected to increase for the majority of countries in each scenario.
source: The force of infection is projected to increase for the majority of countries in each scenario.
evidence: This is supported by the model projections presented in the results.

claim: Central African Republic is one of the countries most likely to see an increase in transmission.
source: Consistently, the Central African Republic is one of the countries most likely to see an increase in transmission, while Liberia and Guinea Bissau have more uncertain projections.
evidence: This is supported by the model projections for specific countries.

claim: Liberia and Guinea Bissau have more uncertain projections for transmission increase.
source: Consistently, the Central African Republic is one of the countries most likely to see an increase in transmission, while Liberia and Guinea Bissau have more uncertain projections.
evidence: This is supported by the model projections for specific countries.

claim: In all scenarios, there is a high probability that the number of deaths and deaths per capita will increase in the African endemic region.
source: In all scenarios, there is a high probability that the number of deaths and deaths per capita will increase in the African endemic region.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of model projections.

claim: The number of deaths per year is expected to increase by 10.0% (95% CrI [−0.7, 34.1]) under RCP scenario 2.6 by 2070.
source: We expect the number of deaths per year to increase by 10.0% (95% CrI [−0.7, 34.1]) under RCP scenario 2.6 or 40.0% (95% CrI [−2.9, 178.6]) under RCP scenario 8.5 by 2070 (see Table 1 for other values).
evidence: This is supported by the model projections shown in Table 1.

claim: The number of deaths per year is expected to increase by 40.0% (95% CrI [−2.9, 178.6]) under RCP scenario 8.5 by 2070.
source: We expect the number of deaths per year to increase by 10.0% (95% CrI [−0.7, 34.1]) under RCP scenario 2.6 or 40.0% (95% CrI [−2.9, 178.6]) under RCP scenario 8.5 by 2070 (see Table 1 for other values).
evidence: This is supported by the model projections shown in Table 1.

claim: The force of infection is assumed to change linearly between 2018 and 2050, and between 2050 and 2070.
source: We assume that the force of infection changes linearly between 2018 and 2050, and between 2050 and 2070.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption stated in the methods.

claim: For RCP scenario 2.6, deaths largely cease increasing after year 2050.
source: For RCP scenario 2.6, deaths largely cease increasing after year 2050, in line with the assumption that RCP 2.6 represents the situation where contributing carbon activities peak by 2030; however, this scenario has been suggested to be 'unfeasible' (Mora et al., 2013; van Vliet et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the model projections shown in Video 1 and citations to Mora et al., 2013 and van Vliet et al., 2009.

claim: RCP scenario 2.6 has been suggested to be 'unfeasible'.
source: For RCP scenario 2.6, deaths largely cease increasing after year 2050, in line with the assumption that RCP 2.6 represents the situation where contributing carbon activities peak by 2030; however, this scenario has been suggested to be 'unfeasible' (Mora et al., 2013; van Vliet et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mora et al., 2013 and van Vliet et al., 2009.

claim: In RCP scenario 8.5, carbon contribution activities are assumed to continue increasing throughout the century.
source: In RCP scenario 8.5, carbon contribution activities are assumed to continue increasing throughout the century.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the RCP 8.5 scenario.

claim: The number of YF deaths predicted in East and Central Africa accelerate after 2050 in RCP scenario 8.5.
source: A potential impact of this is seen in the number of YF deaths predicted by our model in East and Central Africa, which accelerate after 2050.
evidence: This is supported by the model projections shown in Video 1.

claim: Climate change may affect not only the magnitude of YF disease burden but also its distribution.
source: Climate change may affect not only the magnitude of YF disease burden but also its distribution.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results showing heterogeneous changes across regions.

claim: Through the projected changes in both temperature and rainfall, transmission may change heterogeneously across the region.
source: We find that, through the projected changes in both temperature and rainfall, transmission may change heterogeneously across the region.
evidence: This is supported by the model projections showing different changes in different regions.

claim: Temperature change will drive the variation in transmission intensity with rainfall often acting to mitigate.
source: This is emphasised by their individual contribution; in the appendix, we explore the effects of changes in only temperature or rainfall. This illustrates that whilst temperature change will drive the variation in transmission intensity with rainfall often acting to mitigate, in some countries there can be a 'perfect storm' of altering rainfall and temperature leading to increases in transmission that would not occur if only temperature was varying.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis in the appendix examining individual contributions of temperature and rainfall.

claim: In some countries there can be a 'perfect storm' of altering rainfall and temperature leading to increases in transmission that would not occur if only temperature was varying.
source: This is emphasised by their individual contribution; in the appendix, we explore the effects of changes in only temperature or rainfall. This illustrates that whilst temperature change will drive the variation in transmission intensity with rainfall often acting to mitigate, in some countries there can be a 'perfect storm' of altering rainfall and temperature leading to increases in transmission that would not occur if only temperature was varying.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis in the appendix examining individual contributions of temperature and rainfall.

claim: Countries such as Ethiopia and Somalia may become higher priority targets for vaccination due to climate change.
source: Thus, whilst the countries experiencing the highest numbers of deaths will remain high risk, see Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4 for the median distribution of deaths per year, countries such as Ethiopia and Somalia may become higher priority targets for vaccination.
evidence: This is an inference from the model projections showing increased burden in these countries.

claim: The analysis was limited to covariates with projections in 2050 and 2070, namely temperature and precipitation.
source: In order to utilise emission scenario projections, we were limited to covariates with projections in 2050 and 2070, namely temperature and precipitation.
evidence: This is an explicit limitation stated in the discussion.

claim: The adapted model includes temperature range, temperature suitability and precipitation rather than enhanced vegetation and landcover.
source: This meant that we adapted our previous best-fit model (Garske et al., 2014) to include temperature range, temperature suitability and precipitation rather than enhanced vegetation and landcover.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the model adaptation with citation to Garske et al., 2014.

claim: The change in model covariates slightly reduced fit quality, giving an AUC of 0.9004 as opposed to 0.9157.
source: This change slightly reduced fit quality, giving an AUC of 0.9004 as opposed to to 0.9157 (Gaythorpe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis of model fit with citation to Gaythorpe et al., 2019.

claim: Vegetation is a key factor determining habitat of non-human primates.
source: Vegetation is a key factor determining habitat of non-human primates, an element that may not be captured by the temperature suitability index which focuses on the vector A. aegypti.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NHP habitat requirements.

claim: The omission of vegetation factors may lead to an overestimation of the future burden.
source: This omission may lead to an overestimation of the future burden as elements such as desertification and the impact of increasing frequencies of forest fires are not considered (Overpeck et al., 1990; Huang et al., 2016; James et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation about the impact of model limitations with citations to Overpeck et al., 1990, Huang et al., 2016, and James et al., 2013.

claim: Urbanisation has been shown to both reduce disease burden and increase emergence of arboviruses.
source: As such, we omit the human choices that may affect population distributions and behaviour, for example urbanisation which has been shown to both reduce disease burden (Wood et al., 2017) and increase emergence of arboviruses (Gubler, 2011; Hotez, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wood et al., 2017, Gubler, 2011, and Hotez, 2017.

claim: The model does not explicitly include climate scenario-specific migration.
source: In the same way, while our model accounts for migration through use of the UN WPP population data, climate scenario-specific migration is not included in the model.
evidence: This is an explicit limitation stated in the discussion.

claim: The omission of climate scenario-specific migration may mean the model underestimates potential increases in burden due to increased infringing of human environments on the sylvatic cycle.
source: This may mean that we under estimate the potential increases in burden due to increased infringing of human environments on the sylvatic cycle.
evidence: This is speculation about the impact of model limitations.

claim: The manuscript does not explicitly propagate uncertainty in vaccination coverage.
source: Vaccination is the main control method for yellow fever and whilst we account for vaccine coverage and efficacy in this mansucript, we do not explicitly propagate uncertainty in vaccination coverage.
evidence: This is an explicit limitation stated in the discussion.

claim: The model will underestimate the uncertainty in estimates of burden in the future by not propagating uncertainty in vaccination coverage.
source: As such, whilst we focus on the effect of changing transmission, we will underestimate the uncertainty in our estimates of burden in the future.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of model limitations.

claim: The temperature suitability index is informed by A. aegypti and YF-specific datasets on extrinsic incubation period, vector mortality and bite rate.
source: We use A. aegypti and YF-specific datasets to inform the thermal response relationships and thus, temperature suitability index. However, some data, such as information on the extrinsic incubation period are severely limited; we use a dataset of experimental results from 1930s (Davis, 1932).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the data sources with citation to Davis, 1932.

claim: Data on the extrinsic incubation period are severely limited, using a dataset of experimental results from the 1930s.
source: We use A. aegypti and YF-specific datasets to inform the thermal response relationships and thus, temperature suitability index. However, some data, such as information on the extrinsic incubation period are severely limited; we use a dataset of experimental results from 1930s (Davis, 1932).
evidence: This is an explicit limitation stated with citation to Davis, 1932.

claim: The extrinsic incubation period data may be outdated due to current mosquito species potentially adapting to different climates as well as improved experimental procedures.
source: These data may be outdated due to current mosquito species potentially adapting to different climates as well as improved experimental procedures.
evidence: This is speculation about the limitations of the data.

claim: New experimental results concerning the extrinsic incubation period could provide valuable insight into the dynamics of the virus in mosquitoes today.
source: This is a key data gap for YF and new experimental results concerning the extrinsic incubation period could provide valuable insight into the dynamics of the virus in mosquitoes today.
evidence: This is speculation about future research needs.

claim: Yellow Fever is known to have multiple vectors, each contributing to transmission cycles differently.
source: YF is known to have multiple vectors, each contributing to transmission cycles differently (Monath and Vasconcelos, 2015), which are likely to have different thermal responses.
evidence: This is established knowledge with citation to Monath and Vasconcelos, 2015.

claim: Focusing only on the urban vector of YF means the model likely underestimated the uncertainty in the thermal response of the vectors of YF.
source: Focusing only on the urban vector of YF, as we have in this manuscript, means that we will likely under-estimated the uncertainty in the thermal response of the vectors of YF and thus future projections of burden.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of model limitations.

claim: The model assumes a relatively detailed relationship between transmission and temperature but only a simple relationship with rainfall.
source: Additionally, whilst we have included a relatively detailed relationship between transmission and temperature, we have only assumed a simple relationship with rainfall.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the model structure.

claim: Models of thermal response for vectors of diseases such as YF are well parametrised with experimental results.
source: Currently models of thermal response for vectors of diseases such as YF are well parametrised with experimental results; however, this is not yet the case for the influence of rainfall on transmission although there are clear links with aspects such as vector breeding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the state of the field.

claim: The influence of rainfall on transmission is not yet well parametrised with experimental results.
source: Currently models of thermal response for vectors of diseases such as YF are well parametrised with experimental results; however, this is not yet the case for the influence of rainfall on transmission although there are clear links with aspects such as vector breeding.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the state of the field.

claim: The model focuses only on a constant force of infection model which is similar to assuming the majority of transmission occurs as a result of zoonotic spillover.
source: We focus only on a constant force of infection model which is similar to assuming the majority of transmission occurs as a result of zoonotic spillover.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the model assumption.

claim: The assumption that the majority of transmission occurs as a result of zoonotic spillover is supported by recent studies.
source: This assumption is supported by recent studies Gaythorpe et al., 2019; however, the urban transmission cycle, driven by A. aegypti plays a crucial role in YF risk and was responsible for recent severe outbreaks such as that in Angola in 2016.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gaythorpe et al., 2019.

claim: The urban transmission cycle, driven by A. aegypti, plays a crucial role in YF risk and was responsible for recent severe outbreaks such as that in Angola in 2016.
source: This assumption is supported by recent studies Gaythorpe et al., 2019; however, the urban transmission cycle, driven by A. aegypti plays a crucial role in YF risk and was responsible for recent severe outbreaks such as that in Angola in 2016.
evidence: This is established knowledge about YF transmission.

claim: Incorporating climate projections into models that examine multiple transmission routes and thermal responses for multiple vectors would produce a more realistic picture of how the dynamics of YF may change with climate.
source: Incorporating climate projections into models that examine multiple transmission routes and thermal responses for multiple vectors, would produce a more realistic picture of how the dynamics of this disease may change with climate.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: Disease burden and deaths from YF are likely to increase heterogeneously across Africa due to climate change.
source: Here, we examined the specific effects on YF and find that disease burden and deaths are likely to increase heterogeneously across Africa.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the model projections.

claim: There is a need to implement and prepare for new vaccination activities and consolidate existing control strategies in order to mitigate the rising risk from YF.
source: This emphasises the need to implement and prepare for new vaccination activities, and consolidate existing control strategies in order to mitigate the rising risk from YF.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results about policy implications.

claim: Fractional dosing is a useful resort to respond to urban outbreaks in case of vaccine shortage.
source: Intervention through vaccination is the gold standard for YF, and new approaches are being implemented with respect to fractional dosing which is a useful resort to respond to urban outbreaks in case of vaccine shortage (Vannice et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vannice et al., 2018.

claim: Novel vector control measures such as the use of Wolbachia show promise for YF control.
source: Yet, vaccination is not the only potentially effective control for YF, with novel vector control measures such as the use of Wolbachia showing promise, and perspectives to improve clinical management or urban resilience (Rocha et al., 2019; World Health Organization, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rocha et al., 2019 and World Health Organization, 2017.

claim: Effective and sensitive surveillance will be essential to monitor and respond to changing transmission patterns.
source: Finally, in order to monitor and respond to changing transmission patterns, effective and sensitive surveillance will be essential.
evidence: This is an inference about policy implications.

claim: YF occurrence data were collected from the WHO weekly epidemiological record, disease outbreak news, published literature and internal WHO reports.
source: These data were collected from the World Health Organisation (WHO) weekly epidemiological record (WER), disease outbreak news (DON), published literature and internal WHO reports (World Health Organization, 2009; World Health Organization, 1996).
evidence: This is an explicit description of data sources with citations.

claim: The YF occurrence database includes all outbreaks recorded for yellow fever resolved at province level.
source: The database includes all outbreaks recorded for yellow fever and is resolved at province level, any reports that could not be resolved at province level were excluded.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the data.

claim: The WHO African Regional Office YF surveillance database included data from 21 countries in West and Central Africa.
source: Additionally, reports of suspected YF cases were collected in the WHO African Regional Office YF surveillance database (YFSD); this included data from 21 countries in West and Central Africa.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the data.

claim: The YFSD database was based on the broad case definition of fever and jaundice leading to a large proportion of cases attributed to non-YF causes.
source: The database was based on the broad case definition of fever and jaundice leading to a large proportion of cases attributed to non-YF causes and cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses was not considered.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the data limitations.

claim: The incidence of suspected cases can be used as a measure of surveillance effort.
source: However, the incidence of suspected cases can be used as a measure of surveillance effort and is included as a covariate in the generalised linear model.
evidence: This is an explicit description of how the data is used in the model.

claim: Surveillance effort is assumed to be constant over time due to scarcity of data on the subject.
source: We assume this to be constant over time due to scarcity of data on the subject.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption stated in the methods.

claim: Surveys of seroprevalence were conducted in Central and East Africa to assess transmission intensity.
source: Surveys of seroprevalence were conducted in Central and East Africa. We use these to assess transmission intensity in specific regions of the African endemic zone.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the data and its use.

claim: The serological surveys were included only if they represent the population at steady state.
source: The surveys were included only if they represent the population at steady state, as such outbreak investigations were omitted (Garske et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an explicit inclusion criterion with citation to Garske et al., 2014.

claim: In the majority of serological surveys, vaccinated individuals were not included.
source: Additionally, in the majority of surveys, vaccinated individuals were not included; however, in South Cameroon, vaccination status is unclear and so we fit an additional vaccine factor for this survey.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the data and how it was handled.

claim: Vaccination coverage is estimated using data on historic large-scale mass vaccination activities taking place between 1940 and 1960.
source: Vaccination coverage is estimated using data on historic large-scale mass vaccination activities taking place between 1940 and 1960 (Durieux, 1956; Moreau et al., 1999), routine infant immunisation reported by the WHO and UNICEF estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC) (World Health Organization/ UNICEF, 2015), outbreak response campaigns from 1970 onwards which are detailed in the WHO WER and DON (World Health Organization, 2009; World Health Organization, 1996) and recent preventive mass-vaccination campaigns carried out as part of the yellow fever initiative (World Health Organisation, 2016).
evidence: This is an explicit description of data sources with multiple citations.

claim: The vaccination coverage estimation methodology follows Garske et al. and Hamlet et al.
source: The coverage is estimated with the methodology of Garske et al. and Hamlet et al. and is visualised in the polici shiny application (Garske et al., 2014; Hamlet et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garske et al., 2014 and Hamlet et al., 2018a.

claim: All targeted age groups are assumed to have an equal chance of vaccination irrespective of vaccination status.
source: We assume all targeted age groups have an equal chance of vaccination irrespective of vaccination staus.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption stated in the methods.

claim: Demography is obtained from the UN World Population Prospect.
source: Demography is obtained from the UN World Population Prospect (UN WPP) (DoE United Nations, 2017).
evidence: This is an explicit description of data source with citation.

claim: Population data is dis-aggregated to province level by combining UN WPP with estimates of spatial population distributions from LandScan 2014.
source: We dis-aggregate this to province level by combining it with estimates of spatial population distributions from LandScan 2014 (Dobson et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the methodology with citation to Dobson et al., 2000.

claim: The model assumes that the age structure is relatively similar across all provinces in each country.
source: This allows us to estimate population sizes at province level for each year of interest assuming that the age structure is relatively similar across all provinces in each country.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption stated in the methods.

claim: Three main environmental covariates are used within the generalised linear model of YF occurrence: mean annual rainfall, average temperature and temperature range.
source: We use three main environmental covariates within the generalised linear model of YF occurrence: mean annual rainfall, average temperature and temperature range, shown in Figure 6 and listed in Table 2.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the model covariates with reference to Figure 6 and Table 2.

claim: Environmental covariates are gridded data at various resolutions, ranging from approximately 1 km to 10 km, which are averaged at the first administrative unit level.
source: These are gridded data at various resolutions, ranging from approximately 1 km to 10 km, which we average at the first administrative unit level (Nasa LPD, 2001; Xie and Arkin, 1996; Hijmans et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the data with citations.

claim: Projected temperature and rainfall changes under climate change scenarios were obtained from worldclim version 1.4.
source: Projected temperature and rainfall changes under climate change scenarios were obtained from worldclim version 1.4 (Hijmans et al., 2005; Fick and Hijmans, 2017).
evidence: This is an explicit description of data source with citations.

claim: The worldclim data provided the 5th Intergovernmental panel on climate change (IPPC5) climate projections for four Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs): 2.6, 4.5, 6.0 and 8.5.
source: These data provided the 5th Intergovernmental panel on climate change (IPPC5) climate projections for four Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs): 2.6, 4.5, 6.0 and 8.5 (van Vuuren et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the data with citation to van Vuuren et al., 2011.

claim: Projections of the mean global temperature rise by 2046–2065 are 1 or 2 °C for RCPs 2.6 or 8.5, respectively, compared to pre-industrial levels of the 1880s.
source: Projections of the mean global temperature rise by 2046–2065 are 1 or 2 °C for RCPs 2.6 or 8.5, respectively, compared to pre-industrial levels of the 1880s.
evidence: This is established knowledge about climate projections.

claim: By the end of the century, projections suggest a rise of 1 [0.3 to 1.7] or 3.9 [2.6 to 4.8]°C for RCPs 2.6 or 8.5.
source: By the end of the century, these projections suggest a rise of 1 [0.3 to 1.7] or 3.9 [2.6 to 4.8]°C for RCPs 2.6 or 8.5 (Stocker, 2013; Rogelj et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Stocker, 2013 and Rogelj et al., 2012.

claim: Current warming is estimated to be 0.85 °C since pre-industrial levels.
source: Current warming is estimated to be 0.85 °C since pre-industrial levels (Stocker, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stocker, 2013.

claim: Based on current commitments through aspects such as the Paris agreement, scenarios where temperatures are expected to rise by more than 3 °C have been suggested to be most likely.
source: Based on current commitments through aspects such as the Paris agreement, scenarios where temperatures are expected to rise by more than 3 °C have been suggested to be most likely (Sanford et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sanford et al., 2014.

claim: A recent study omitted the RCP 2.6 scenario as it is unlikely now to occur.
source: As such, a recent study omitted the RCP 2.6 scenario as it is unlikely now to occur (Mora et al., 2013; van Vliet et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mora et al., 2013 and van Vliet et al., 2009.

claim: Projected mean rainfall, maximum temperature and minimum temperature are available for each RCP scenario in years 2050 and 2070.
source: Projected mean rainfall, maximum temperature and minimum temperature are available for each RCP scenario in years 2050 and 2070.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the available data.

claim: The midpoint and range of the temperature are taken as inputs for the model of YF occurrence.
source: We take the midpoint and range of the temperature as inputs for the model of YF occurrence, where the midpoint temperature is used to calculate the temperature suitability index.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the methodology.

claim: The model does not model changes in climate prior to 2018, instead using Worldclim baseline estimates representative of conditions from 1960 to 1990.
source: We do not model changes in climate prior to 2018, instead using Worldclim baseline estimates described as representative of conditions from 1960 to 1990 (Hijmans et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the methodology with citation to Hijmans et al., 2005.

claim: The components of the temperature suitability index are estimated from YF-specific sources of information on extrinsic incubation period, vector mortality and bite rate for A. aegypti.
source: We estimate the components of the temperature suitability index from YF-specific sources of information on extrinsic incubation period, vector mortality and bite rate for A. aegypti, the urban vector of YF (Davis, 1932; Tesla et al., 2018; Hamlet et al., 2018b; Mordecai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the data sources with multiple citations.

claim: Bite rate data was included from both Mordecai et al., 2017 and Martens, 1998 which both describe A. aegypti.
source: We included bite rate data from both Mordecai et al., 2017 and Martens, 1998 which both describe A. aegypti.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the data sources with citations.

claim: Vector mortality was estimated from the experimental data of Tesla et al., 2018.
source: Finally, vector mortality was estimated from the experimental data of Tesla et al., 2018.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the data source with citation.

claim: The thermal response models are estimated within a Bayesian hierarchical framework in order to capture uncertainty.
source: Whilst we focus only on thermal response of the urban vector of YF due to data availability, we estimate the thermal response models within a Bayesian hierarchical framework in order to capture some of the uncertainty that we miss from examining one vector species.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the methodology.

claim: The model of YF occurrence is reformulated to accommodate nonlinear dependence on temperature and rainfall.
source: We reformulate an established model of YF occurrence to accommodate nonlinear dependence on temperature and rainfall (Garske et al., 2014; Jean et al., 2020; Gaythorpe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the model with citations.

claim: The model is coupled with established results from a transmission model of serological status to estimate transmission intensity across the African endemic region at baseline.
source: We couple this with established results from a transmission model of serological status to estimate transmission intensity across the African endemic region at baseline/current environmental conditions .
evidence: This is an explicit description of the methodology.

claim: Temperature and rainfall are known to have implications on both the vectors of YF and the distribution of the non-human primate reservoir.
source: Temperature and rainfall are known to have implications on both the vectors of YF and the distribution of the non-human primate reservoir (Reinhold et al., 2018; Cowlishaw and Hacker, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reinhold et al., 2018 and Cowlishaw and Hacker, 1997.

claim: The effect of temperature on vectors is highly non-linear with increased mortality seen at very low and high temperatures.
source: However, the effect of temperature, particularly on vectors, is highly non-linear with increased mortality seen at very low and high temperatures; as such, we include the range in temperature as a covariate of our occurrence model as well as the non-linear temperature suitability index (Mordecai et al., 2017; Tesla et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mordecai et al., 2017 and Tesla et al., 2018.

claim: The temperature suitability is modeled using a function of temperature for the mosquito biting rate, the extrinsic incubation period and mortality rate for the mosquito.
source: We model this using a function of temperature for the mosquito biting rate, the extrinsic incubation period and mortality rate for the mosquito which we combine to calculate the temperature suitability based on the Ross-MacDonald formula for the basic reproduction number of a mosquito-borne disease (Macdonald, 1957).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the methodology with citation to Macdonald, 1957.

claim: The functional form used to model temperature suitability can be parameterised solely from data specific to YF.
source: We continue to use a form which can be parameterised solely from data specific to YF (Hamlet et al., 2018b; Garske et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hamlet et al., 2018b and Garske et al., 2013.

claim: Alternative formulations of temperature suitability have been published in the context of other arboviral infections.
source: However, alternative formulations have been published in the context of other arboviral infections (Mordecai et al., 2017; Ryan et al., 2019; Brady et al., 2014; Brady et al., 2013; Tjaden et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The transmission intensity is assumed to be a static force of infection.
source: The transmission intensity is assumed to be a static force of infection, akin to the assumption that most YF infections occur as a result of sylvatic spillover (Garske et al., 2014; Gaythorpe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the model assumption with citations.

claim: The force of infection is assumed to be constant in each province over time and age.
source: The force of infection is assumed to be constant in each province over time and age.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption stated in the methods.

claim: The models of temperature suitability and YF report are estimated together within a Bayesian framework using Metropolis-Hastings Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling with an adaptive proposal distribution.
source: We estimate the models of temperature suitability and YF report together within a Bayesian framework using Metropolis-Hastings Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling with an adaptive proposal distribution (Andrieu and Thoms, 2008; McKinley et al., 2014; Roberts and Rosenthal, 2009; Sherlock et al., 2015; Tennant and McKinley, 2019).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the methodology with multiple citations.

claim: The model propagates uncertainty in the estimation of the GLM from the thermal response models as well as that from the seroprevalence into the resulting transmission intensity estimates.
source: We propagate uncertainty in the estimation of the GLM from the thermal response models as well as that from the seroprevalence into the resulting transmission intensity estimates.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the methodology.

claim: The estimation, analysis and manuscript were all performed or written in R version 3.5.1.
source: The estimation, analysis and manuscript were all performed or written in R version 3.5.1, ridgeline plots were generated with packages ggplot2 and ggridges (R Development Core Team, 2014; Wickham, 2016; Wilke, 2018; Garnier, 2018).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the software used with citations.

claim: In order to assess future changes in force of infection and disease burden, ensemble climate projections of temperature change and precipitation are incorporated.
source: In order to assess future changes in force of infection, and thus disease burden, we incorporate ensemble climate projections of temperature change and precipitation.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the methodology.

claim: Burden is estimated by calculating the proportion of infections who become severe cases and then, of those, the proportions that die, using published case fatality ratio estimates.
source: We estimate burden by calculating the proportion of infections who become severe cases and then, of those, the proportions that die, using published case fatality ratio estimates (Johansson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an explicit description of the methodology with citation to Johansson et al., 2014.

claim: Burden estimates are compared with a baseline scenario assuming the same demographic conditions and vaccination levels as the climate change scenarios but no change in climate variables over time.
source: We compare burden estimates with a baseline scenario assuming the same demographic conditions and vaccination levels as the climate change scenarios but no change in climate variables (precipitation and temperature) over time.
evidence: This is an explicit description of the methodology.

claim: The predicted probability of a YF report is positively informed by temperature suitability.
source: The predicted probability of a YF report is positively informed by temperature suitability with the median posterior predicted distribution shown in Figure 2 (left).
evidence: This is supported by the model results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The prediction of the median incubation period at 25°C is in line with that of Johansson et al., 2010 who found it to be 10 days [2.0 - 37] days.
source: The prediction of the median incubation period at 25°C is in line with that of Johansson et al., 2010 who found it to be 10 days [2.0 - 37] days.
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work cited as Johansson et al., 2010.
